stem: A client takes cholestyramine for hyperlipidemia and several other oral medications. Which instruction should the nurse provide?

options.A: Take other oral medications at least 1 hour before or 4–6 hours after cholestyramine to reduce the risk that cholestyramine will impair their absorption.
options.B: Take all oral medications at exactly the same time as cholestyramine because the resin does not bind other drugs in the gastrointestinal tract.
options.C: Inject cholestyramine subcutaneously because oral administration creates clinically important drug-binding interactions.
options.D: Timing is irrelevant because cholestyramine is systemically absorbed before it can affect other oral medications.

rationale: A is correct. Current FDA labeling states that cholestyramine may bind other concurrently administered drugs and impede their absorption. The label recommends taking other drugs at least 1 hour before or 4 to 6 hours after cholestyramine, or at as great an interval as possible. B and D contradict this labeled interaction. C is incorrect because cholestyramine is an oral resin that acts within the gastrointestinal tract rather than being given by injection.
educational_objective: Teach clients taking cholestyramine to separate other oral medications by at least 1 hour before or 4–6 hours after the resin because cholestyramine can bind medications in the gut and reduce their absorption.
source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling via DailyMed
source_document_title: Cholestyramine for Oral Suspension, USP Prescribing Information
source_locator: Drug Interactions/Precautions: cholestyramine may bind other drugs given concurrently. Label recommendation: take other drugs at least 1 hour before or 4 to 6 hours after cholestyramine, or at as great an interval as possible, to avoid impeding absorption. The label also notes that cholestyramine is confined to the gastrointestinal tract rather than systemically absorbed.
source_claim_supported: Cholestyramine can bind concurrently administered oral drugs and reduce absorption; current labeling recommends separating other oral medications by at least 1 hour before or 4–6 hours after cholestyramine.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: identify medication interactions, provide administration teaching, and reduce medication-related risk.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — cholestyramine drug interactions and timing
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw class-level statement around named cholestyramine and replaced the vague phrase 'timing separation is generally recommended' with the exact current FDA-label interval of at least 1 hour before or 4–6 hours after. The final item avoids extrapolating identical timing rules to every bile-acid sequestrant.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against a current 2026 DailyMed cholestyramine label.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A reproduces the exact label interval and mechanism. B denies the interaction. C uses the wrong route. D falsely states systemic absorption and no timing effect.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; separate other oral medications by the labeled interval.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; concurrent administration can impair absorption.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; cholestyramine remains in the GI tract and can bind other drugs there.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Naming cholestyramine avoids assuming that every bile-acid sequestrant shares exactly the same separation interval.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address administration timing, route, or absorption interactions.
audit_findings.blueprint: Medication-interaction teaching fits Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked the exact 1-hour-before/4–6-hours-after interval, GI confinement, and class-generalization risk. No second defensible answer remained.
